findings.claim: Hitachi Gallman MS: $528M plant for 10-160 MVA units up to 230 kV. Construction is to begin late 2026 and production in 2029. No groundbreaking had been reported as of Oct 11, 2026.
findings.detail: Announced Sep 15, 2026. The press release describes construction start as future (late 2026). No MDEQ notice was found.

findings.claim: Gallman is partly a relocation. It sits ~6.5 miles from Crystal Springs and is more than twice its size, and Crystal Springs production is to move to Gallman when it is complete. Net new US capacity is therefore roughly one Crystal Springs, not the full Gallman output.
findings.detail: This matches Utility Dive's 'double US production' framing: if a site 2x Crystal Springs replaces Crystal Springs, the net add is about 1x. Computed reasoning, not a company statement of net units. Whether the Crystal Springs building is closed, sold or repurposed is unknown.

findings.claim: Gallman job counts conflict: the company says more than 700 jobs, while Big Energy News says more than 1,600.

HD Hyundai Electric broke ground on Montgomery plant #2 on Mar 6, 2026. The plant is ~312,000 sq ft inside the existing site, costs $200M, and adds 50% to EHV output with 765 kV build and test capability.
findings.detail: 200 new jobs. Total HD-HPT investment in Montgomery reaches $277M. This is the only plant in the set with both a dated groundbreaking and an EHV scope.
findings.entity: HD Hyundai Electric (Hyundai Power Transformers USA), Montgomery AL

findings.claim: HD Hyundai's completion date conflicts: the company says April 2027, while the Montgomery Chamber says the plant opens mid-2027.

findings.claim: VTC's Rincon GA expansion has slipped and been scaled back. The Nov 2025 announcement promised ~70% more production about one year after a Jan 2026 start. A later VTC groundbreaking release cites a 50% increase in installed capacity and completion in March 2027.

findings.claim: The Rincon scope includes new Vapor Phase Drying equipment, plus vertical winding machines, core-building machinery and a transformer prep area. VPD typically uses a solvent, so it is the item most likely to need a GA EPD air permit or modification. No such permit was found.

The second site was not identified. This resolves the baseline's 'start date unverified', though no exact first-production date was found. Computed: $25M / 200 jobs = $125k capex per job.

result.analysis:
Permits do not yet confirm any plant's schedule. No state air permit, construction-stormwater NOI or throughput/VOC limit was found for any of the nine plants (se-permits-none-indexed). The permit databases are not crawlable, so the next step is direct database queries or records requests.

Non-permit evidence still separates the plants:
- **Physically underway:** HD Hyundai Montgomery #2 (groundbreaking Mar 6, 2026; se-hdh-groundbreak), Hyosung Memphis (Nov 24, 2025; se-hyosung-groundbreak), Hitachi Alamo bushings (Aug 2025; se-alamo), Howard Ellisville (Apr 2026, due end-2026; se-howard-timing) and VTC Rincon.
- **Least verified:** the two largest job counts. Hitachi Gallman has not started; construction begins late 2026 for 2029 output (se-gallman-scope). VTC Muscle Shoals has no confirmed groundbreaking or site work since its May 2026 announcement, yet guides to January 2028 output (se-vtc-ms-scope).

Four points bear on a would-be builder:
1. **The incumbent wave is smaller and later than the headlines.**
   - Gallman partly replaces Crystal Springs, so the net addition is about one Crystal Springs, not a full new plant (se-gallman-replaces-crystal-springs).
   - VTC Rincon slipped from ~+70% by end-2026 to +50% by March 2027 (se-vtc-rincon-slip).
   - HD Hyundai's date already reads April or mid-2027 depending on the source (se-hdh-date-conflict).
   - Treat every 2027-29 date as likely to slip 3-6 months. That slightly widens the window for an entrant shipping in 2028.
2. **Howard is moving up-market fast.** Ellisville goes from 168 MVA/230 kV to 250 MVA/345 kV by end-2026 (se-howard-ratings), and a separate $237M, 450-job program runs through ~2030 (se-howard-2025-mda). That is direct competition in the 10-100 MVA band an entrant would grow into, and it makes Howard harder to buy cheaply.
3. **Re-using existing buildings is the proven low-capex route.**
   - Eaton is converting a former Belk distribution center with a $10M state retrofit grant (se-eaton-brownfield).
   - Central Moloney is already producing single-phase pole-mounts in a leased 140k sq ft spec building for about $25M (se-cmi-operating).
   - Computed capex per announced job: ~$125k for Central Moloney versus ~$486k for Eaton and up to ~$754k for Gallman (se-capex-per-job-computed). This supports the buy-or-convert entry over a $340-530M greenfield.
4. **Air permitting looks manageable but unverified.** VTC's Rincon scope includes vapor-phase drying (se-vtc-rincon-vpd). An entrant should budget a minor-source or synthetic-minor air permit for VPD solvent and varnish/paint VOC, and should pull a comparable permit from GA EPD or MDEQ to size the limits before choosing a site.

result.analysis:
No plant schedule in this domain could be verified against an agency permit, certificate of occupancy or stormwater record. Agency portals (VA DEQ myDEQ, MCAQ, MCAQD, TCEQ) are not search-indexed, and NC DAQ's statewide list did not surface Prolec or PTT [hitachi-sb-no-permit, ncdaq-list-negative]. Every date below is still company guidance, cross-checked against incentive records and press.

Three points matter for a would-be builder.

1. **The segment a newcomer would target is filling up faster than the baseline showed, including outside the Southeast.**
   - PTT, owned by Quanta, is adding a 150k sq ft pad-mount plant in Raeford that ships in early 2027 [ptt-raeford-padmount].
   - ERMCO skipped construction and bought a finished 566k sq ft West Valley shell for $91M (~$161/sq ft computed) for 2027 3-phase output [ermco-az-91m]. That weakens the "site outside the Southeast" edge in the Southwest specifically.
   - Giga (1,000+ units) and JST (1,000/yr from 2027) add more medium-voltage and pad-mount volume [giga-houston-status, jst-wytheville-site].

2. **Buying or converting an existing building is now the dominant fast route.** ERMCO (spec shell), VanTran (former Sherwin-Williams DC) and Heron (286k sq ft warehouse) all took it [vantran-waco-incentives, heron-morgan-hill]. Unleased spec space remains next to ERMCO [waddell-spec-shells]. For distribution-class work, which needs no 375-ton cranes or 120 ft bays, an entrant can copy this path and ship in roughly 12-18 months. This supports the round-1 advice to buy or expand rather than build greenfield.

3. **Large-power capacity keeps slipping, but that gap is not one a newcomer can reach.**
   - Siemens Charlotte production moves to 2027 [siemens-clt-latepost].
   - Hitachi South Boston only broke ground in June 2026, so 2029 looks more likely than 2028 [hitachi-sb-groundbreak, hitachi-sb-2029].
   - Niagara was still in IDA approval in September 2026 [niagara-ecida, niagara-nypa-scope].
   - Only Prolec Goldsboro has an investment deadline (Dec 31, 2027) consistent with its stated date [prolec-gso-deadline].

**JST's likely Jinpan ownership is the most decision-relevant new lead** [jst-jinpan-link, W]. If EO 14420 adopts an ownership/control test, up to 1,000 units/yr of pad-mount supply in Virginia, plus JST's Yangzhou-built imports, could be cut off. That would open room for a domestic pad-mount entrant.

**Incentive benchmarks:**
- Niagara: ~9.4% of capex from ECIDA plus NYPA (computed).
- Heron: CalCompetes $26.4M on >$100M.
- VanTran: Enterprise Zone up to $960k.
- PTT: $400k rail grant.

Local packages are modest. Plan on 3-10% of capex, not a decisive subsidy.

result.analysis:
Main finding: the incentive filings show subsidies are too small to decide where a transformer plant gets built, and show labor and existing buildings matter more. Disclosed state and local awards come to only about 0.8-6.4% of capex [computed-incentive-intensity]:
- NC JDIGs are capped near $14K per job and pay out over 12 years, only after jobs and investment are verified [nc-jdig-prolec-goldsboro-2025, nc-jdig-siemens-2024].
- PTT got only an $800K One NC Fund grant on $102.5M [nc-onenc-ptt-raeford-2025].
- Virginia's $29.4M MEI grant is the richest found, and Hitachi still needed a workforce-housing subsidy [va-mei-hitachi-south-boston].
- A newcomer should treat incentives as a few points of capex, not as a reason to pick a site. Payments that only follow job and investment targets also add clawback-style risk if the ramp slips.

Wage floors are the most useful number for a business plan. Contracted average wages are $64,949-71,912, 52-56% above the county average, even in low-wage NC counties [computed-wage-benchmarks]. Hitachi's housing deal and AccelerateMS training point the same way: labor is the binding constraint in the Southeast [ms-mflex-hitachi-gallman].

Capex per job runs about $420K-$975K for new or expanded power-transformer capacity, and about $1.4M per added unit/yr at Niagara [computed-niagara-productivity, ecida-niagara-2026]. The low outliers are VanTran ($20-33M for 430k sq ft) [tx-vantran-waco] and Eaton, which is retrofitting an existing 861k sq ft building with a $10M state grant for building improvements [sc-ccced-eaton-jonesville]. Both support the round-1 advice to buy or reuse rather than build greenfield. A 10-year IDA PILOT in New York shows a non-Southeast site can be economic [ecida-niagara-older].

The capacity wave is larger than the baseline shows:
- Siemens added a $421M NC program in Feb 2026, partly LPT [siemens-nc-421m-2026].
- Hyosung's 2025-26 tranches total $208-238M (computed), which settles the $157M figure as one tranche [hyosung-investment-reconcile].
- VTC's reported ~$300M is low for a 1,100-job, 2-500 MVA plant, so its actual capex is still uncertain [vtc-muscle-shoals-capex].

Correction: the baseline's separate Mitsubishi Memphis plant appears to be the plant Hyosung bought in 2019, so Memphis capacity is double-counted [mitsubishi-memphis-stale].

Still missing: the job ramps by year and the clawback terms. These sit in the agreement PDFs listed under gaps.

result.analysis:
Buyer-level evidence now exists, but almost all of it comes from small municipal utilities, and most of it is W-grade AI summaries of council minutes.

**Prices**
- Small single-phase units cost about $3,000 each (median $3,025, n=5) [calc-price-medians].
- New three-phase pad-mounts run about $28-32/kVA at 1.5-2 MVA and about $89/kVA at 225 kVA [bid-newrichmond-2025, bid-newcordell-2026]. Most of the value per unit sits in larger units.
- Rebuilt pad-mounts sell at near-new $/kVA [bid-coldwater-rebuilt-2025, bid-niles-2025]. Buyers are paying for speed, not cost.

**Contract terms and competition**
- Contract terms are tightening on suppliers. GUC accepts only firm prices and awards on total ownership cost [terms-guc-2026], and Pasadena caps escalation at CPI [terms-pasadena].
- But Ocala paid a $1.1M PPI adjustment on 105 MVA autotransformers [bid-ocala-ppi-2026], and Milton-Freewater accepted surcharges [bid-miltonfreewater-2026].
- An entrant needs escalators. Utilities that insist on firm or CPI-capped prices will push input risk onto the maker.
- Competition at the low end comes from imports and resellers:
  - Eaglerise underbid US distributors by 18-23% in Lafayette's 2026 three-phase pad-mount bid [bid-lafayette-2026].
  - Korean makers Kerec, Sungjin and Taihan are named contractors on Austin Energy's $200M distribution supply award [bid-austin-200m-2026].
  - Distributors (Wesco, Resco, Irby, Gresco, Border States, Anixter) and Sourcewell are the channel to small munis. A new maker must get onto their line cards.

**Lead times**
- **Substation and power:** the median quoted or estimated lead time is about 130 weeks, and buyers pay premiums or waive bidding to get anything faster [calc-substation-lt-median, bid-fpua-2026, bid-oakridge-2025].
- **Distribution, on Howard's claim of under 20 weeks:**
  - The only firm new-unit quote in 2026 is 12-13 weeks, for Vermillion's 16 units in August [bid-vermillion-2026], which supports Howard.
  - A February 2026 supplier testimony cited 40-50 weeks for new pad-mounts [lt-reman-testimony-2026], and Newton warned of more than a year [bid-newton-2026].

**Implications for a builder**
- Single-phase stock is likely loosening, which is consistent with Howard. That segment should be avoided.
- The three-phase pad-mount lead time, the segment the entry thesis targets, is still unproven. One firm quote does not trip the "walk away if bids show under 20 weeks" trigger. The ~130-week substation backlog supports the later 10-100 MVA path, but that is where Korean makers such as LS Electric are already shortlisted [bid-snopud-gsu-2026].
- Before committing, pull three-phase bid tabs that list delivery weeks from the joint-action agencies (ElectriCities, FMPA, AMP, MMPA).

result.analysis:
Margins at transformer makers were expanding through Q2 2026, not being squeezed, but the gains come mostly from operating leverage and price/mix rather than a wider gross spread. Forgent's adjusted EBITDA margin hit 24.4% in Q4 FY26 (+640bp YoY) and is guided to ~24% for FY27 [fps-fy26-results, fps-fy27-guide]. Its computed gross margin slipped from ~36.9% to ~35.1% [fps-gross-margin-computed]. Hammond's gross margin of 31.5% is roughly flat YoY (the base is disputed), while EBITDA rose to 16.4% [hps-q2-26, hps-gm-yoy-conflict]. Power-transformer makers show the clearest pricing power:
- HD Hyundai Electric posted a 25.1% operating margin, with North America revenue up only 10%, which means price and mix rather than volume [hdhe-q2, hdhe-na-orders].
- Hyosung's margin rose 490bp to 15.7% [hyosung-q2].
- GE Vernova Electrification gained +700bp organically [gev-elec-q2].

Hubbell Utility is the warning case: low-single-digit price only offset raw-material, tariff and inflation costs, and its margin was flat [hubb-us-q2].

For a would-be entrant:
1. **The profit pool is large.** Prolec earned ~25% EBITDA and sold at 13.9x; over half of the $9,656M price is goodwill [gev-prolec-margin, gev-prolec-ppa]. Scaled incumbents earn 16-25% EBITDA, which gives a newcomer room to price below them and still make money.
2. **Margins depend on data centers and are now growing through volume.** Data centers are 59% of Forgent's revenue [fps-mix-capacity]. Hammond's backlog is falling quarter on quarter, and Canadian pricing is turning competitive [hps-backlog-canada]. That is consistent with round 1's view that distribution and dry-type capacity is catching up.
3. **Capacity is being added fast.** Forgent claims enough to support ~$5B of revenue against $2.5B guided [fps-mix-capacity], and Hammond's Monterrey plants are ramping. That supports entering by buying or expanding an existing plant rather than building greenfield.
4. **Q2 results probably understate the input-cost hit.** Copper is up 45% since November, so Q3 prints in late October and November are the test.

Cliffs disclosed no GOES price, and Butler's +25% GOES output arrives only in 2028 [clf-q2-goes]. Contracts with escalators and secured core supply remain prerequisites.

findings.claim: The Aug 26, 2026 order is Executive Order 14421, 'Declaring a National Emergency to Secure the United States Bulk-Power System'. It was published as FR Doc 2026-17843 on Aug 31, 2026, and DOE's RFI cites it as EO 14421. Sources that call it EO 14420 are wrong.
findings.detail: This run confirmed the number and the FR doc number on federalregister.gov. The page cite 91 FR 55995 and govinfo DCPD-202600561 come from round-2 verify notes and were not re-checked here. Sources using 14420: the baseline market map, Crowell and H&K (per baseline), APPA (per round 2), mgrid.org and Potencia Partners. The baseline line 'EO 14420 (cited as 14421 by some firms)' has it backwards.

findings.claim: EO 14421 reuses the EO 13920 definition of the bulk-power system: it includes transmission lines rated 69 kV or more and excludes 'facilities used in the local distribution of electric energy'.
findings.detail: Corroborated by Pillsbury, Troutman ('at or above 69 kV') and APPA. EO 13920 used the same wording (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2020-05-04/pdf/2020-09695.pdf). Round 1 only inferred a 2020-style definition; this confirms it. No MVA threshold was found in any source.

findings.claim: The order defines 'bulk-power system electric equipment' as items used in bulk-power system substations, control rooms, or power generating stations. Law-firm summaries list transformers, inverters, BESS, generators and turbines, SCADA and RTUs, industrial control systems and breakers, plus associated software, firmware, remote access and lifecycle update mechanisms.
findings.value: Substations, control rooms, generating stations; no MVA floor
findings.detail: The FR search excerpt stopped before this definition, so the exact 2026 list (for example whether it repeats EO 13920's instrument transformers, reclosers and voltage regulators) is unverified. DOE's RFI asks how to define the term further. Sources: Troutman, DWT, pv magazine (Aug 27 headline: transformers, inverters, circuit breakers), APPA (software, firmware, remote access, lifecycle maintenance).

findings.claim: A 'Covered Foreign Entity' is a country subject to an arms embargo or sanctions regime under ITAR 22 CFR 126.1, or a person owned by, controlled by, or subject to the jurisdiction or direction of such a country's government. It also covers any person the Secretary of Energy, consulting the Secretary of War, the DNI and the APNSA, finds is engaged in detrimental conduct.
findings.detail: The ownership/control wording comes from Pillsbury (https://www.pillsburylaw.com/en/news-and-insights/eo-foreign-produced-bulk-power-system.html); the FR excerpt matches it. The order uses 'Covered Foreign Entity', not EO 13920's 'foreign adversary' and 15 CFR 7.4 framing. Pillsbury stresses that foreign origin alone does not make a transaction prohibited. Legal500 says the determination can rest on CFE-linked design, manufacture or supply. This test can reach Chinese-owned plants in Mexico and probably Chinese-owned US entities. Whether a US-built unit counts as 'foreign-produced' is an open RFI question.

findings.claim: The '24 countries' are the ITAR 126.1 sanctions and arms-embargo countries: China plus Afghanistan, Belarus, Congo, Central African Republic, Cuba, Cyprus (through Sep 30, 2026), Eritrea, Ethiopia, Haiti, Iran, Myanmar, Iraq, Lebanon, Libya, Nicaragua, North Korea, Russia, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Syria, Venezuela and Zimbabwe.
findings.detail: Computed check: 23 named countries + China = 24. This resolves round 2's doubt about why the count is not the 6-country 15 CFR 7.4 list. Cyprus's listing ends Sep 30, 2026, so the count may now be 23 (inference). DWT names China (incl. Hong Kong), Iran, Venezuela and Russia as examples. None of the main transformer exporters to the US besides China (Mexico, Korea, Brazil, India, Canada, EU, Japan, Turkey) is on the list.

findings.claim: A prohibition needs four things: foreign-produced BPS equipment, a foreign country or national with an interest in the transaction, a transaction begun after Aug 26, 2026, and a DOE finding of undue risk of sabotage, unauthorized access or supply disruption. DOE must issue rules 'as needed' within 120 days.
findings.detail: Undue-risk language comes from National Law Review. Dates conflict: most sources say about Dec 24, 2026 (computed: Aug 26 + 120 days); Lexology says about Dec 27. DOE's webinar said nothing is barred until DOE makes vendor or transaction determinations, and DOE 'has not adopted licensing, waiver, pre-qualification' criteria (round-2 verify notes, https://www.energy.gov/documents/executive-order-14421-rfi-webinar-transcript). mgrid.org (W): the order 'bans nothing yet'.

findings.claim: The order is not grandfathered. DOE may impose conditions on foreign BPS equipment acquired or installed before Aug 26, 2026, including monitoring, physical or network isolation, and replacement or removal. At the Sep 16 webinar, DOE answered 'potentially' when asked whether installed equipment could be affected, and only after the required findings.
findings.detail: Troutman says DOE may require disconnection or removal. DWT's webinar recap gives the 'potentially' answer. Bracewell flags retroactive reach. Existing equipment is a separate RFI topic (Section D per summaries). This bears on replacement demand if DOE orders swaps of Chinese units installed in 2024-26.

findings.claim: The order does not mention data-center substations by name; data centers appear only in its rationale. Counsel read it in different ways: Pillsbury says it appears to focus on grid-facing rather than behind-the-meter facilities, while DWT says equipment below 69 kV can still be covered as substation or control equipment and that the transmission-distribution boundary needs facility-specific analysis.
findings.detail: DWT flags data-center BESS, inverters, controls and UPS as raising questions. DOE's CESER page and Utility Dive cite AI, data centers and advanced manufacturing as the reason for the order. RFI question A-2 asks about UPS supporting critical infrastructure and about backup and small generators, which shows DOE is considering widening scope toward data-center electrical rooms. Inference: a data-center main substation interconnected at 69 kV or above is probably in scope; MV pad-mounts on the customer side are probably out, unless DOE's rules widen scope.

result.analysis:
For someone planning to build transformers, the order text changes how the round-1 plan should be read.

**Distribution is likely outside the order.** EO 14421 (not 14420) reuses EO 13920's definition word for word: the bulk-power system starts at 69 kV, and local distribution is excluded [bps-def-69kv, eo-number-14421]. The 0.5-10 MVA pad-mount and unit-substation segment recommended in round 1 mostly sits at or below 34.5 kV on the distribution or customer side, so the order probably gives it no direct shelter. Round 1 set a walk-away condition: DOE's rules exclude distribution. On the evidence so far, that condition is more likely than not to be met [data-center-scope].

**Two openings could widen it.** RFI question A-2 asks about facilities that combine transmission and distribution functions, and about UPS and backup generators. DWT also argues that substation equipment below 69 kV can be caught [rfi-structure, data-center-scope]. Any December rule that adopts these readings would pull data-center electrical rooms into scope.

**Substation transformers are where the order bites.** These are 69 kV and above, roughly 10-100 MVA, including data-center main substations interconnected to the grid. There is no MVA floor [bps-equipment-def], so a 20 MVA, 138/34.5 kV unit is covered if it is grid-facing. That supports the round-1 'later path to 10-100 MVA' and argues for building 69-138 kV capability earlier.

**The ownership test is real but has a gap.** A Covered Foreign Entity includes any person owned or controlled by a listed government, across 24 ITAR countries [cfe-ownership-test, 24-countries-list]. That likely catches Chinese-owned plants in Mexico. Whether a US-built unit from a Chinese-owned plant such as JST counts depends on how DOE defines 'foreign-produced', which it has not yet done. No allied exporter (Korea, Mexico, Brazil, India) is covered, so the substitution demand goes mainly to them and to incumbents, not automatically to a new entrant.

**Installed equipment is not grandfathered.** DOE may require monitoring, isolation or removal of units already in service [installed-equipment]. That is a possible but unquantified source of replacement demand for 2024-26 Chinese substation units.

**Nothing is banned yet.** Each prohibition needs a transaction-specific finding of undue risk, and the rules are due 'as needed' around Dec 24-27 [trigger-and-timing]. Expect a review-and-licensing regime, not a blanket ban, so utilities' preference for domestic or allied suppliers will be a matter of de-risking, not a legal requirement.

**The lobbying picture is still unknown.** As of Oct 12, no NEMA, EEI, APPA, NRECA, Data Center Coalition, ACP, SEIA, OEM or utility comment was public [docket-comments-status]. The asks on thresholds, grandfathering and prequalification cannot yet be gauged; recheck the docket in late October.

findings.detail: The baseline's ~$36B STEP estimate was not found in any ERCOT document. The official 2024 RTP figure is $32.99B, and including live reconductoring narrows the gap with the 345-kV option to $1.35B. The $36B may be a later escalation, but this run found no source for it. Also in the 2024 RTP report: https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2025/01/27/2024-regional-transmission-plan-rtp-345-kv-plan-and-texas-765-kv-strategic-transmission-expans.pdf

findings.detail: This is the first sourced per-site transformer rule for the ERCOT 765-kV build. ERCOT gives no grand total.

findings.claim: COMPUTED: if all 12 new STEP 765-kV substations get transformers per ERCOT's rule, the plan needs ~27 765/345-kV banks. As single-phase banks with one spare per site, that is ~81 active single-phase units plus ~12 spares, ~93 units in all. The MVA total would be ~65 GVA.
findings.detail: Inputs: 3 sites x 3 banks + 9 sites x 2 banks = 27 banks. The 27 x 2,403 MVA = 64,881 MVA assumes every bank matches Hillje's rating. Assumptions, not sourced: every new 765-kV substation also transforms to 345 kV; each ~2,400 MVA bank is three single-phase ~800 MVA autotransformers, the usual US 765-kV practice; one spare phase per site. By region: Eastern = 3+3+3+2 (Martin Lake assumed 2) = 11 banks, ~33 units + ~4 spares. Permian = 8 x 2 = 16 banks, ~48 units + ~8 spares.

findings.claim: ERCOT's large-load interconnection requests reached ~474 GW in June 2026, ~90% data centers, up from ~410 GW on Mar 26, 2026 (~87% data centers). 198 GW was requested in Q1 2026 alone, while ~9,456 MW is approved to energize.
findings.value: 474 GW queue; 9,456 MW approved to energize
findings.detail: The 410 GW and Q1 figures are from RTO Insider (https://www.rtoinsider.com/129421-ercot-large-load-requests-soar-again/). Utility Dive also cited 438 GW in a June 22, 2026 piece, a different cut-off. The 9,456 MW was reported from ERCOT's August Monthly Operational Overview; the nearest URL found is the June MOO (https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/07/17/ERCOT-Monthly-Operational-Overview-June-2026.pdf). Gov. Abbott ordered an audit and ERCOT delayed Batch Zero. The queue is speculative: 474 GW is more than 5x ERCOT's record peak.

findings.claim: COMPUTED (assumption-based): each GW of data-center load implies ~9-22 HV/MV substation power transformers and ~460-890 MV/LV unit-substation or pad-mount units of 2.5-3 MVA. Applied to ERCOT's ~9.456 GW approved to energize, that is ~85-210 HV/MV power transformers and ~4,400-8,400 MV/LV units.
findings.value: ~460-890 MV/LV units per GW; ~9-22 HV/MV units per GW
findings.detail: Inputs, all assumptions except the 9,456 MW: 1 GW at 0.9 power factor = 1,111 MVA. MV/LV low end: 1,111/3 MVA x 1.25 (N+1) = 463 per GW. High end: 1,111/2.5 MVA x 2 (2N A/B feeds) = 889 per GW. HV/MV: 1,111/150 MVA, about 7.4, rounded up to N+1 gives ~9; 1,111/100 MVA with 2N gives ~22. 9.456 x 463 = 4,378; 9.456 x 889 = 8,406. Do not apply this to the 474 GW queue, which is mostly speculative. This segment (0.5-10 MVA) is the round-1 recommended entry point.

findings.claim: At 2Q 2026, GE Vernova's gas backlog plus slot reservations was 116 GW: 53 GW firm equipment backlog and 63 GW of slot reservation agreements, up from 100 GW. It targets at least 125 GW by year-end, a 20 GW/yr production rate in Q3 2026 and 24 GW in 2028, and is working toward 30 GW in 2030.
findings.detail: Sources the baseline's GE Vernova gas backlog. In Q2, 10 GW of SRAs converted to firm orders and 3 GW shipped (https://www.utilitydive.com/news/ge-vernova-gas-turbine-backlog-climbs-to-116-gw/826039/). Company totals: orders $24.2B (+88% organic) and backlog $176B. Computed: 116 GW / 20-24 GW/yr = ~4.8-5.8 years of production. The US share and the split between heavy-duty and aeroderivative units are not disclosed in the material read.

findings.claim: GE Vernova booked $2.7B of data-center orders in its Electrification segment in 2Q 2026, after $2.4B in 1Q. Year-to-date data-center orders exceed $5B, more than double the 2025 total. Electrification orders were $6.3B (+66% organic), book-to-bill ~1.7, revenue $3.6B.
findings.detail: Sources the baseline's $2.7B claim. The figure is from the earnings call transcript; the press release (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1996810/000199681026000147/gevpressrelease2q26.htm) gives >$5B YTD. Q1 was $2.4B (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001996810/000199681026000063/gevpressrelease1q26.htm). Management cited equipment backlog above $40B. Electrification now includes Prolec GE transformers, so this is a direct read on data-center transformer and switchgear pull.

findings.claim: Siemens Energy booked 15 GW of gas turbine orders in FQ3 FY2026 (quarter ended Jun 30, 2026): 73 gas turbines, 25 large and 48 industrial. Its backlog reached 69 GW after 6 GW shipped, lead times are 3+ years, and the CEO sees an addressable market of ~120 GW/yr, about half in the US.
findings.value: 69 GW backlog; 15 GW / 73 units ordered in quarter
findings.detail: Computed: 15 GW / 73 units = ~205 MW per unit, blended across large and industrial. Unlike GE's 116 GW, Siemens' 69 GW is firm backlog without reservations, so the two are not directly comparable.

findings.claim: Mitsubishi Heavy's large-frame gas turbine backlog is ~35 GW, up from 23 GW a year earlier. It booked 10 large-frame orders in FQ1 FY2026 (Apr-Jun 2026), 4 for the US and 6 for Japan. In FY2025 it sold 35 large-frame units totaling 16 GW.
findings.detail: Computed: 16 GW / 35 units = ~457 MW per large-frame unit. One secondary source cites a 32 GW backlog. MHI sees a 70-100 GW global market in 2026 vs ~100 GW in 2025.

findings.claim: COMPUTED: the three OEMs' ~220 GW of gas backlog and reservations (116 + 69 + 35) implies roughly 480-1,600 generator step-up transformers worldwide. At ~50% US share, that is ~240-800 US GSUs delivered over ~2026-2031, or about 50-160 a year.
findings.detail: Inputs: 220 GW / 0.457 GW per unit (MHI large-frame average) = ~481 turbines; 220 / 0.205 (Siemens FQ3 blended average) = ~1,073 turbines. GSUs per turbine = 1.0 (simple cycle) to 1.5 (2x1 combined cycle adds one steam-turbine GSU per two gas turbines). Range: 481-1,610 worldwide. The US share of ~50% uses Siemens' CEO's market split as a proxy. GE's figure includes 63 GW of non-firm SRAs. Timing assumes ~5-6 years of OEM output. Large GSUs are a segment round 1 advised a newcomer to avoid; aeroderivative and industrial units (~35-50 MW) use smaller GSUs, which a 10-100 MVA entrant could address.

findings.claim: EIA expects 6.3 GW of new gas-fired capacity in 2026: 3.3 GW combined cycle and 2.8 GW combustion turbines, with over 80% in TX, OK, OH, TN and FL. The largest plants are Orange County Advanced Power Station in Texas (1,158 MW) and Trumbull Energy Center in Ohio (900 MW).
findings.detail: AEO2026 projects 365-430 GW of cumulative gas additions to 2050 depending on case (https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/aeo/pdf/AEO_Narrative.pdf). 2026 is a small year next to the OEM backlogs, so most turbine-driven GSU demand lands in 2027-2031. Unit-level 860M data for a GSU count was not obtained.

findings.claim: NREL projects that in-service US distribution transformer capacity in 2050 will be 160-260% above 2021 levels. DOE puts the current stock at ~60-80 million units and over 3 TW. Average residential transformer size rises more than 150% by 2050, and commercial ~120%.
findings.detail: The stock figure is from DOE (https://www.energy.gov/oe/rd-efforts-address-transformer-supply). CISA's NIAC report quotes 160-280%, likely a typo. Per Utility Dive, ~55% of residential units are near end of life. NREL names aging and electrification as the largest drivers. No 2026 update was found.

findings.claim: COMPUTED: NREL's range implies 2050 distribution capacity of ~7.8-10.8 TW, or ~4.8-7.8 TW if read as 160-260% of 2021. That means ~62-269 GVA/yr of net additions. Replacing the 60-80M-unit stock alone implies ~1.5-2.7M units/yr.
findings.detail: Inputs: 3 TW x 2.6 to 3.6 = 7.8-10.8 TW; (7.8-3)/29 = 166 and (10.8-3)/29 = 269 GVA/yr; lower reading (4.8-3)/29 = 62 GVA/yr. Replacement: 60-80M units over a 30-40 year life (assumed) = 1.5-2.7M units/yr. Because average unit size rises 120-150%, capacity grows much faster than unit count, which favors larger 3-phase units over single-phase pole-mounts.

result.analysis:
Mostly the evidence moves the transmission bull case into countable units, and those units are not ones a newcomer can make.

ERCOT has now written down its transformer rule [ercot-step-xfmr-rule]. Applied to 12 new 765-kV substations, it gives ~27 765/345-kV banks: roughly 80-95 single-phase EHV autotransformers, each of order 800 MVA [ercot-step-xfmr-total-computed]. The Eastern Backbone accounts for ~11 of the 27 banks, in service 2030-2032 [ercot-eastern-backbone, hillje-spec]. PJM and MISO add only a handful of identifiable 765-kV substations so far [pjm-2024-w1, pjm-2025-w1, miso-t21-scope, miso-beci-transource-bhe], with MISO landing in 2032-2034.

That is under ~150 EHV units over 2029-2034 for the three big plans. This market is lumpy, needs qualification, and belongs to Hitachi, Siemens Energy, HD Hyundai and Hyosung, which reinforces the round-1 advice to avoid EHV. Approval risk persists: ALJs recommended denying some Permian lines, competitive bidding may re-open procurement, and the Aug 28, 2026 CCN approvals rest on a weak (W) source [puct-permian-ccn-aug2026, mgrid-competitive-bid].

Gas generation implies ~240-800 US GSUs over ~2026-2031, about 50-160 a year [gsu-from-turbines-computed, gev-gas-backlog, siemens-energy-gt, mhi-gt]. The large-frame share is again a segment for incumbents. Siemens' 48 industrial turbines in one quarter point to a real stream of smaller GSUs, roughly 30-100 MVA, which fits the round-1 '10-100 MVA later' path.

The strongest unit signal for the recommended entry segment is data-center load. GE Vernova's Electrification data-center orders were $2.7B in Q2 and over $5B year-to-date [gev-dc-electrification]. ERCOT has ~9.5 GW approved to energize against a 474 GW speculative queue [ercot-large-load-queue], and PJM adds ~66 GW of peak by 2036 [pjm-load-forecast-2026]. At ~460-890 MV/LV units per GW, ERCOT's approved load alone implies thousands of 2.5-3 MVA units [dc-load-to-units-computed]. This rests on assumptions and needs checking against real site designs.

NREL's projection points the same way: capacity grows far faster than unit count because units get larger [nrel-dist-demand, nrel-units-computed], which favors 3-phase pad-mount and unit-substation production over single-phase.

Five of the six baseline claims now have sources. The ~$36B STEP figure is not supported; ERCOT's own figure is $32.99B.

findings.claim: DOE disclosed the first 48C Round 1 recipients in April 2024: 35 projects in 20 states with about $1.93B of allocations. Grid components such as transformers were among the categories, and Eaton was also named. One guide says Round 1 critical-materials awards included electrical-steel projects.
findings.detail: The electrical-steel claim comes from a W-grade guide (scoutcities.com) and is not tied to a named company. Names are disclosed only after certification, which can take up to two years, so other transformer or steel recipients may still be undisclosed.

findings.claim: 48C Round 2 offered up to $6B, with ~$2.5B reserved for energy communities. It listed grid manufacturing (distribution and large power transformers, subcomponents, materials, HV breakers, HVDC cable) as a priority. Allocations announced in early 2025 were described as final.
findings.detail: Sources disagree on the totals. Scout says $6B went to 140 projects. Crux says ~$2.5B went to energy-community projects, 'totaling $4 billion across both rounds', apparently meaning the energy-community share only. No transformer recipients from Round 2 were named. WSGR called Round 2 'potentially final'.

findings.claim: No 48C allocation capacity appears to remain in 2026. The IRA's $10B authority was fully allocated across Round 1 ($4B) and Round 2 ($6B), and no third round was found.
findings.value: $0 remaining (computed: $10B authority minus $4B Round 1 minus $6B Round 2)
findings.detail: Computed. The $4B Round 1 total is IRA statute and general knowledge, not taken from these search results. The $6B Round 2 figure comes from Honigman and Energy Communities. A new entrant cannot plan on 48C unless Congress adds authority, or unless an allocated project forfeits and the credit is re-allocated (no evidence of that).

findings.claim: No DOE Loan Programs Office (renamed Office of Energy Dominance Financing, EDF) loan or conditional commitment to a transformer or grid-equipment manufacturer was found for 2025-2026. In Jan 2026 EDF restructured, revised or eliminated $83.6B of the $104B in Biden-era obligations, and it lists grid/transmission and manufacturing among its priorities.
findings.detail: Precedents for equipment-maker financing exist outside the grid. In June 2026 EDF conditionally committed $17.5B in loan facilities for long-lead equipment for up to 10 AP1000 reactors. In April 2026 it committed up to $263M to SHINE Chrysalis. Grid lending has gone to utilities (Jan 2025: 8 conditional commitments, $22.92B), and the JCP&L commitment was terminated on Aug 20, 2025 (JCP&L S-4).

result.analysis:
For a would-be builder, federal money is mostly a promise, not cash, as of Oct 2026.

**DPA.** The legal basis is strong [fed-pd-2026-10-scope]:
- PD 2026-10 names transformers, electrical core steel and manufacturing tools.
- It waives the usual Sec. 303 findings.
- DOE is already pointing to Sec. 303 purchase commitments in its distribution-transformer RFI [fed-dpa-in-efficiency-rfi].

But no Title III solicitation, offtake or award was found six months on [fed-dpa-no-solicitation]. A W-grade source says the program machinery was still being built in July. It also flags a statutory sunset on Sep 30, 2026 [fed-dpa-machinery-sunset]. That claim is unverified, but if true it could leave the PD without money. Treat DPA as upside optionality and keep it out of the base case.

**48C is effectively closed.** Siemens Energy's Charlotte LPT plant got $18.3M [fed-48c-siemens-charlotte]. Grid equipment was a named Round 2 priority. But both rounds ($4B + $6B) are allocated and described as final [fed-48c-round2-final, fed-48c-exhausted]. A 2026 entrant cannot plan on 48C without new legislation.

**LPO/EDF** has not lent to any grid-equipment maker [fed-edf-no-grid-maker]. Its grid lending went to utilities, and it has since cut Biden-era commitments. The Westinghouse long-lead-equipment facility shows EDF will finance supply chains when politically favored. A transformer-plant application is plausible but untested.

**Federal purchasing is real but narrow:**
- WAPA sole-sourced a large-power-transformer blanket purchase agreement to Virginia Transformer [fed-wapa-vtc-bpa]. That makes VTC more valuable as an acquisition target and shows the power marketing administrations will contract with US-based independents.
- USACE is setting up a decade-long multi-award IDIQ for custom hydro GSUs, funded by BPA and open to Reclamation [fed-usace-hydro-idiq]. The notice says plainly that LPT makers are capacity-constrained.
- These are custom GSU and LPT units, the segment the round-1 synthesis tells a newcomer to avoid.
- Federal hydro buys often go through installing integrators rather than to manufacturers [fed-reclamation-glen-canyon-benchmark].

There is no strategic reserve or standardized bulk-buy program [fed-reserve-none]. A DPA Sec. 303 purchase commitment would be the only live route to a buyer-of-last-resort.

**Net:** a distribution or pad-mount entrant should expect almost no direct federal demand or subsidy in 2026-27. The federal levers that matter are the EO 14420 rules (Dec 2026) and any DPA purchase commitment. Both need watching before committing capital.

result.analysis:
The headline: the pad-mount newcomer the baseline called 'private' is Chinese-controlled. Jinpan's 2024 annual report defines JST USA as JST Power Equipment, Inc. (formerly Jinpan International (U.S.A.)) [jst-is-jinpan-subsidiary]. JST USA booked RMB 1.3B of revenue in H1 2026, about 37% of Jinpan's total [jst-usa-h1-2026-financials]. It owns plants in Lake Mary FL and Wytheville VA [jst-lake-mary-plant], and its parent claims ~5,000 MVA a year of capacity in Mexico [jinpan-mexico-capacity, W]. Eaglerise is a second case: its US and Mexico plants are ramping [eaglerise-us-mexico-plants]. No North American plants were found for Sieyuan, TBEA, Chint and the others [other-chinese-na-plants-not-found].

For a builder, this makes the design of the EO 14420 rules a direct swing factor. If the rules test ownership or control, a Chinese-owned pad-mount supplier already selling ~$360M a year into the US (annualized, computed) becomes exposed in exactly the 3-phase pad-mount segment a newcomer would target. If they test only place of manufacture, JST competes as 'domestic'.

The pool of independent makers that could be bought has shrunk:
- Central Moloney has been owned by Wind Point since 2023 [central-moloney-wind-point].
- Southwest Electric went to SGB-SMIT in 2025 [southwest-electric-sgb-smit].
- PCEP went to Mill Point/Voltaris for $50M [pioneer-pcep-sale].
- Delta Star and Sunbelt Solomon are pending with PE buyers [delta-star-signed-sep1-pending, sunbelt-solomon-pending-past-target].

What remains family- or founder-owned is Howard (~4,000 staff, too large) [howard-size], VTC (>$6B ask, no 2026 progress) [vtc-sale-no-2026-news], Maddox (~400 staff, fast-growing) [maddox-profile], ELSCO and Meta Power. Central Moloney is the most actionable target, since a PE seller is likely to want an exit in 2027-29.

Exits look credible. At least seven active PE or strategic acquirers have done deals since 2023 (Blackstone/MacLean, TJC, Wind Point, Mill Point, SGB-SMIT, GE Vernova, IPS). The valuation spread is wide:
- The scale leader cleared at about 13-14x 2025E EBITDA [prolec-implied-multiple, computed].
- Lower-middle-market manufacturing averages 5.9-8.8x [lmm-manufacturing-multiples, W].

That gap rewards a buy-and-build that reaches scale before the 2027-29 capacity wave. The caution is that no private transformer deal has published EBITDA. VTC's unconsummated $6B also warns that sellers' asking prices may be running ahead of what buyers will clear.

Giga raised only ~$30M of venture capital and funded growth largely from customer deposits [giga-funding]. That suggests a deposit-funded, data-center-anchored entry can work with modest equity.

result.analysis:
Labor is the hidden capacity limit, and the 2027-28 wave will compete for the same thin pool a newcomer needs. Official 6-digit headcount (QCEW 335311) is still missing [qcew-335311-not-retrieved], so whether real headcount is growing is not yet proven.

**Size of the trained pool**
- In 2023 the whole electrical equipment industry (NAICS 3353) employed only 3,600 coil winders. That was down 1.6% from 2022, and the wage was flat at $21.78/hr, below the all-industry winder mean [oews-coil-3353-2023, oews-coil-3353-2022].
- The trained pool is therefore small and was not growing through 2023, even as prices rose.
- Pools are thin at state level too: Tennessee had 920 winders across all industries [oews-coil-state-2023]. Memphis is concentrated, but Hyosung is adding 363 jobs there [oews-coil-msa-2021, hyosung-memphis-hiring].

**Size of the coming demand**
- The seven target announcements total about 4,388 jobs, mostly hiring in 2027-28 [announced-jobs-7-plants].
- That is 1.2 times the industry's 2023 winder headcount. If the commercial estimate of ~18,600 employees in 335311 is roughly right, it is also over 20% of the sector [siccode-335311-estimate].
- Incumbents are already working around the constraint:
  - Hitachi plans to nearly double South Boston headcount and is building 136 employee housing units on county-donated land [hitachi-sb-hiring].
  - Eaton has lined up readySC state pre-hire training [eaton-jonesville-hiring].
  - Siemens runs a standing requisition for its Charlotte plant [siemens-charlotte-hiring].
- Broader factory labor tightness adds pressure, though that evidence is weaker [mfg-labor-surveys-2026, jolts-mfg-openings-jul2026].

**Implications for a builder**
1. Budget for winder wage inflation and a long training ramp. Your hiring window overlaps Eaton, ERMCO, Siemens and VTC Rincon in 2027 and Hitachi and VTC Muscle Shoals in 2028.
2. Site the plant away from these clusters. Round 1's advice to avoid the Southeast is reinforced: ERMCO, in Arizona, is the only target plant outside the region [ermco-az-hiring].
3. Buying an existing plant buys a trained workforce, which is arguably worth more than its floor space.
4. Rincon now completes in March 2027 at +50%, not in 2026 at +70% [vtc-rincon-revision]. This shifts a little more incumbent supply into 2027, the year a buyer-entrant would be ramping.

Before committing, pull QCEW 335311 and the OEWS 2024-25 MSA data for candidate sites.

findings.detail: Datamyne describes 8504.23.0080 as liquid dielectric transformers exceeding 100,000 kVA, and 8504.23.0040 as exceeding 10,000 but not exceeding 100,000 kVA. The 2017 Federal Register LPT scope notice (https://public-inspection.federalregister.gov/2017-26071.pdf) lists both 0040 and 0080 for transformers of 60,000 kVA and above, which fits 0080 being the >100 MVA line. Aggregators (Paxai, Credlix, Dripcapital) suggest the 10-100 MVA band may now be split into 0041 (10,000-59,999 kVA) and 0045 (59,999-100,000 kVA). That is W and does not affect 0080. Plausibility flag (computed): $2.77B / 2,268 units = about $1.22M average declared value per unit, and NextMSC's Mexico value is about $0.71M per unit. Both are low for >100 MVA units, which could mean disassembled or partial shipments are counted as units, or the counts are mis-scoped. Not resolved.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIABLE: no independent source confirms 2,268 units ($2.77B) in 2025, 2,901 units in the 12 months to Jun 2026, Mexico 630 / Brazil 343 / Korea 323, or China at about 2.2%. The only other source that repeats these figures (Financial News, Oct 12, 2026) cites NextMSC.
findings.detail: The figures are internally consistent (computed): 630 + 343 + 323 = 1,296, which is 57.1% of 2,268 and matches NextMSC's 57%. 2,901 / 2,268 = +27.9%. 2.2% of 2,268 is about 50 Chinese units. Financial News (https://www.fnnews.com/news/202610120701047050) repeats Mexico 630, Brazil 343 and Korea 323 from NextMSC, and its headline says Korea ranks first by US import value. That fits Mexico leading on units but at a low unit value. USITC pub 5531 snippets gave only MVA capacity data (Korean producers' available capacity 50,980 / 44,090 / 31,057 MVA in 2021-23), not import units. Keep the figures labeled as vendor-derived.

findings.detail: The Federal Register notices 2026-15181 and 2026-15274 (Jul 28, 2026) carry the same exemption: inputs such as auto parts already under 232 are exempt. 10% applies to economies with a forced-labor import ban, a reciprocal-trade commitment or a partial regime, and 12.5% to the rest. result.analysis:
Most of the claims the round-1 case rests on hold. The weakest ones are the import-volume series and the tariff on cores, and both feed the entry thesis directly.

Confirmed from primary sources:
- The Korea antidumping rates are 0% for HD Hyundai and Iljin and 4.32% for LS and Hyosung [verify-korea-ad-final]. So large power units from Korea face only 15% Section 232 plus small or zero antidumping duty [verify-s232-annex-iii]. That keeps the advice to avoid large power and EHV intact.
- Prolec GE's $9,656M is an accounting total: $5,254M cash plus a $4,402M remeasured stake. It is not a cash price for 100% [verify-prolec-consideration]. Use it as a valuation marker only.
- The PPI levels are right [verify-ppi-wpu117409, verify-ppi-pcu335311]. The July jump in WPU117409 was +4.6% in one month after three flat months, and August's PCU335311 was flat. This supports round-1's view that prices move in steps driven by cost pass-through. The +8.7% YoY is still unchecked.
- Howard's under-20-week claim is real [verify-howard-leadtimes]. APPA's 2025 survey median of 50 weeks and Howard's own earlier 1-4 year statements [howard-leadtime-contrast] mean distribution lead times have either collapsed or are being understated by an interested party. Bid data remains the deciding test.

Not verified:
- The NextMSC unit counts [verify-nextmsc-units]. The HTS label is correct [verify-nextmsc-hts-scope], but the average declared value of about $1.22M per unit is low for >100 MVA. The 'import boom in >100 MVA' and 'China is only 2%' points should stay labelled as vendor-derived until Census HS-10 is pulled.
- Korea's Jan-Jul 2026 figure [verify-korea-uhv-2026-janjul]. The 2025 base of $738.28M is solid [verify-korea-uhv-2025].

Biggest open risk: the Section 232 treatment of cores [verify-s232-cores]. Round 1 assumed 25%. One reading of the April annex puts cores at 50% in Annex I-A, and the June amendment's placement is unconfirmed. If cores pay 50% while finished distribution units pay 25% and large units 15%, the tariff penalty on buying imported cores is worse than modelled. That strengthens the case for a domestic core supply contract, and Butler is still only on track for 2028 [verify-cliffs-butler]. Weirton's cancellation is confirmed [verify-cliffs-weirton]. The general Section 301 exclusion for Section 232 goods is confirmed [verify-s301-232-exclusion].
